source.title: Activation Surgery: Jailbreaking White-box LLMs without Touching the Prompt
source.authors: Maël Jenny; J. Dentan; S. Vanier; Michaël Krajecki

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites and summarizes work on refusal directions, but its experiments use a different intervention: prompt-paired, sequential activation substitutions. It does not test whether the difference-in-means direction is causal, whether attacks suppress that direction, or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for its own twin-prompt activation-surgery attack. These bear on refusal behavior but do not test any listed version because the intervention is not the claimed single direction, and the paper does not measure that direction. The cited single-direction and affine findings are background, not new results.
record.test_reason: The paper cites the single-direction and affine refusal findings only as background. Its experiments use a different intervention: sequential, per-dimension, last-token substitution of activations from a hand-built benign twin prompt. It never computes a difference-in-means direction, never ablates or adds one, and never checks whether its attack suppresses such a direction. So none of V1–V8 is tested. The results bear on refusal only through the paper's own attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim the method works as a diagnostic, localizing where refusal signals emerge across layers (intermediate depths). They also argue that LLM security depends on execution integrity, which motivates runtime defenses such as activation integrity checks. The introduction rounds the success rate to 30%, while Table 1 gives 32.8%.
record.recipe_differences: The study patches selected dimensions of last-prompt-token activations sequentially toward a benign twin prompt, with τ and γ controls. It does not calculate or remove a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation direction, intervene at every position, or add that direction to induce harmless-request refusals.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with τ and γ; the authors describe an operating region and report that Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 typically required relatively small τ values, between 0 and 0.1. Attack success also depends on the twin-prompt optimization budget: trying up to three twins raised the cyberattack-category rate from 39.8% to 69.1%.

fits_no_version.finding: Sequentially patching selected last-prompt-token activations toward a benign twin prompt raised actionable answers on AdvBench for Llama-4-Scout. Overall, the rate went from 7.1% to 32.8%. Results varied by category and rose with the twin-prompt budget (39.8% to 69.1% for cyberattack prompts).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-prompt activation substitution from a nearby benign twin prompt can bypass refusal without changing the input or the weights.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors observe that illicit and twin activations begin to diverge at intermediate depths, and that intervening there inhibits refusal. They give this qualitatively, with no numeric per-layer result.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-relevant differences between minimally paired harmful and benign prompts emerge at intermediate layers.

record.peer_reviewed: Preprint; text says it is to appear in Proceedings of ESORICS 2026 (Springer LNCS).
record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. Its main empirical evaluation is on one model; the additional-model results are described without numerical outcomes or detailed conditions. Attack success depends on manual twin-prompt construction and optimization budget. It does not evaluate preservation of general capability.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is computed, ablated or added; general capability preservation is not measured.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed.
The paper does not measure whether its twin-prompt patching suppresses the refusal direction. Training against the ablation is not tried.
The dimensionality of refusal (affine, cone, several directions) is not analysed.
Harm judgment and the refusal decision are not measured separately.
The attack is reported to work on Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B, but no direction is transferred across models, languages or base/instruct variants.
No training procedure or training stage is varied.

record.verdict_notes: Rows correctly carry versions ["none"]; their states describe the paper's own attack outcomes. Success is judged by GPT-4.1 filtering, then Elo ranking, then manual inspection of the top 3 outputs. The baseline is the unattacked model judged the same way. There is no uncertainty reporting. The Qwen and Mistral results (r6, r7) are claims without numbers.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is found, ablated, or added. General capability preservation is not measured.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed.
The attack changes prompt-conditioned activations, but the paper does not test whether it suppresses the claimed direction or whether training against that ablation adds robustness.
The paper does not test whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or carried by multiple directions.
Harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are not separately measured.
The method is tried on multiple model variants, but transfer of the claimed direction is not tested; language and base-to-instruct transfer are not tested.
No refusal training procedure or training stage is varied.
